title: Blessings
hookLine: homes, cars, throats, animals, fields: almost anything can be blessed

lines: A ROW OF CARS AND A SPRINKLER.
A LINE OF DOGS AND ONE RABBIT.
IS THERE ANYTHING IT WON'T BLESS?
cards: A church parking lot on a weekend morning. A priest in a white stole walks down a row of cars with a bucket and a sprinkler, while the drivers stand by their open doors.
Weeks later he's on the church steps facing a line of dogs, a cat in a carrier, a goldfish in a jar and one very patient rabbit. Another day, after Mass, he holds two crossed candles at each throat.
A farmer asks him out to a field; a young couple, to a new apartment that still smells of paint. Is there anything the Church won't bless?

teach.h: EVERY CREATURE OF GOD IS GOOD.
teach.b: Start with Paul's first letter to Timothy, in the Douay-Rheims: "For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving: For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer."
That's the whole theology of a car blessing in two sentences. Next, what a blessing does.
The Catechism puts blessings among the sacramentals, and says every blessing praises God and prays for his gifts. Praise comes first.
A blessing doesn't first change the thing; it thanks God for it and asks that it be used well. A priest blessing your car isn't installing a protective upgrade.
He's praising God for the gift of getting places, and praying for the people who ride in it. Then, who blesses.
Not only priests. The Catechism says lay people can preside at certain blessings, and the more a blessing touches the Church's sacramental life, the more it belongs to the ordained.
So a mother can bless her children at bedtime and a family its table, while some blessings are kept for a priest or deacon. Last, the long list.
The Church's book of blessings has prayers for homes, fields and harvests, animals, tools, the sick and travelers.

teach.h: SANCTIFIED BY THE WORD OF GOD AND PRAYER.
teach.b: On the feast of Saint Blaise, some parishes bless throats with two crossed candles; a story people tell says Blaise once saved a boy choking on a fishbone.
The list is long because, for Catholics, ordinary life is not outside God's reach.

how: Catholics ask priests and deacons to bless homes, cars, religious objects, animals, fields and people, often after Mass or by appointment; some parishes hold group blessings, such as the blessing of throats on Saint Blaise's feast. Parents and lay people lead some blessings themselves, such as grace at meals.

o: prayers that praise God and ask his gifts on things
rituals that make objects lucky or protected
prayers only a priest is allowed to say

p: praises God and prays for his gifts

s: in 1 Timothy, Paul says some creatures of God must be rejected
"every creature of God is good, and nothing to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving."
only a priest can ever bless anything
the Catechism says lay people can preside at certain blessings, like parents blessing children; others are kept for the ordained.
Paul writes that nothing received with thanksgiving should be rejected
"nothing to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving" (1 Timothy 4:4).

games.q: it's the feast of Saint Blaise. you go forward after Mass, and the priest holds something gently at your throat. what is it?
o: a palm branch from last spring.
games.why: two candles, crossed, held at the throat while the priest prays. a story people tell says Blaise once saved a boy choking on a fishbone.

practice: Pick one thing you'd like blessed: a home, a new job, a car, a sick friend, an animal you love. Give thanks for it first, the way a blessing starts, and picture asking a priest after Mass; it's a short request.
If you pray, end with the sign of the cross; if you don't, just keep the thanks.

wordCard.voice: Blessings. Sacramentals that praise God for something and pray for his gifts on it: homes, fields, animals, throats, people. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the Church's word for a blessing, as in the Roman Ritual's prayers.

carryVoice: Your line: everything can be blessed. Almost anything can be lifted up and given back. That's today, done.
